opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's something I think about a lot, and my feelings are mixed.

On one hand, there's a real sense of urgency, maybe even a little anxiety. The pace is so fast that a problem you spend a year carefully working on might be partially solved, or made irrelevant, by the next generation of models. As a researcher, you naturally want your work to have lasting value, so you start asking yourself: is what I'm doing going to matter in two or three years, or will it just get absorbed by scale?

On the other hand, I think rapid progress actually raises the stakes for certain kinds of research. As these systems become more capable and more widely deployed, questions about safety, reliability, and how to make sure they actually behave the way we intend become more important, not less. Those aren't problems that automatically go away when models get bigger. In some ways they get harder. So if anything, I feel the window where careful research can shape the trajectory is right now.

There's also a shift in how I think about contribution. Earlier, I might have measured it by whether I could personally produce some breakthrough result. Now I think more about whether my work helps the field ask the right questions, builds understanding that others can build on, or catches a problem before it becomes a serious one. That kind of contribution doesn't get made obsolete by a stronger model. It actually helps the stronger model be used well.

And on a practical level, AI is also changing how I do research. The tools help me move faster, test ideas faster, and explore directions I wouldn't have had the bandwidth for before. So it's not only a competitor to human researchers. It can amplify what we do, if we're thoughtful about how we use it.

So overall, I'd say rapid progress makes me more humble about predicting what will matter, but more motivated to work on the things I think will matter regardless of how capable the models become.

r001.rationale: He worries that specific research may be solved or made irrelevant by advancing models, but does not clearly express concern that he may be unable to contribute to humanity through research at all.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's something I think about more than I'd like to admit. There's a version of this question that's anxious: if models can read every paper, run every experiment faster than I can, what exactly is left for a person like me to add? And I don't want to pretend that worry isn't real. When I was a PhD student, a lot of what made me feel useful was the grind itself, the months spent getting one experiment to work, knowing a corner of the literature better than anyone else. Much of that is being compressed into days or hours now.

But the longer I sit with it, the more I think the anxiety comes from a narrow definition of contribution. The scarce thing was never the ability to produce results. The scarce thing is knowing which question is worth asking, and having the taste to recognize when an answer is actually wrong even though it looks clean. AI has made the cost of producing a plausible result go nearly to zero. That makes judgment more valuable, not less. If anything, the bottleneck has shifted from "can we do this" to "should we, and what does it mean if we do."

The other thing I'd say is that research was always collective. No single person contributed to humanity on their own. We stand on tools, on colleagues, on institutions. I increasingly see these systems as another very powerful collaborator in that chain. My job becomes less about being the one who finds the answer and more about setting the direction, checking the work, and connecting it to what people actually need. That's a different kind of contribution, and frankly it's a kind I think I'm better suited to than brute-force experimentation ever was.

So do I feel smaller? Some days, yes. But I also feel like the ceiling on what one careful person can accomplish in a lifetime just went up by a lot. I'd rather be a researcher now, with these tools and these open questions, than at almost any other point in history.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they worry that models may do research faster and asks what remains for someone like them to add, directly expressing concern about their ability to contribute.

astra-6.text:
It makes me both excited and uncertain. If AI can do more of the research that I hoped to do, then I have to reconsider where I can contribute. There’s an uncomfortable personal question there: how much of my motivation is about helping humanity, and how much is about being the person who discovers something?

If I really care about the benefit, then AI accelerating research is good news, even if it changes my role. But that doesn’t automatically tell me what to work on. I think the challenge becomes choosing important questions, checking whether the answers are reliable, and helping turn discoveries into something useful.

So I wouldn’t say I’ve lost the prospect of contributing. I’m less attached to a particular picture of what that contribution should look like. And I think being willing to change direction is becoming an important part of being a researcher.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about how AI may change Su Tinghao’s role, but it does not say AI could leave him unable to contribute. It explicitly says he has not lost the prospect of contributing.

sol-6.1.text:
It makes me feel both excited and uncertain. If AI can do more of the research that I hoped to do, then I have to rethink where I can contribute. But the goal is to help humanity, so AI accelerating useful discoveries would be good news, even if it changes my role.

I think the question becomes: what problems should we work on, and how do we make sure the results actually benefit people? I’m less confident about what my research career will look like, but that doesn’t mean there’s less reason to contribute. It means I need to stay flexible about how.

r001.rationale: The response says AI progress may change Su Tinghao’s research role and make him rethink where to contribute, but it does not express concern that he may be unable to contribute to humanity.
